personal.name: Chain Reaction — Real-Time Multiplayer Game
personal.tagline: A server-authoritative real-time multiplayer game: a Node.js WebSocket server owns every board, turn and cascade, so the client can only ask — never decide.
description: Built a real-time multiplayer Chain Reaction game where the backend is the single source of truth: a Node.js + TypeScript WebSocket server owns board state, turn order, cascading explosions, elimination and match teardown, while the Next.js 15 / React 19 client renders broadcasts and sends nothing but player intent.

Designed the rules engine as a pure, I/O-free TypeScript module (createBoard, getCriticalMass, getNeighbors, applyMove, isEliminated) so the identical code path runs inside the server, in a standalone smoke script, and later in replay or AI opponents.
Modeled matchmaking as per-configuration queue buckets keyed by board preset x player count (4 presets, 2–20 players per match), alongside private rooms joinable through ambiguity-free invite codes.
Persisted only completed matches — Supabase Postgres through Prisma behind a repository layer — and broadcast game_over to players before any write, so a database outage costs stats, never gameplay.

Shipped XP/level progression with per-mode leaderboards, JWT email/password auth plus Google OAuth via Supabase (accounts linked by email), a 30-second reconnect grace window, and a WebSocket protocol documented in lockstep with shared TypeScript types.

Hardened for production before launch: fail-closed config, per-IP and global rate budgets, connection caps, a room reaper, XP anti-farm velocity limits, and a Docker + Fly.io deployment gated by GitHub Actions CI.
architecture: Client: Next.js App Router with a four-state phase machine (lobby -> queued -> playing -> gameover) owned by a single useGameWebSocket hook. The client never computes a next board — it renders what the server broadcasts.
Server: ws gateway -> router -> typed handlers -> services -> repositories. Every inbound frame is validated by a Zod schema at the edge; malformed frames are dropped rather than trusted.
Live state: four module-level Maps (sockets, connection identities, queue buckets, rooms + player->room index). Nothing per-move touches the database.

Durable state: Postgres via Prisma in a strict repository pattern — Prisma is imported by repositories only, never by controllers, services, handlers or game logic. Schema covers players, matches, match participants and a per-mode stat projection for leaderboard reads.
Delivery: multi-stage Docker build on Fly.io for the long-lived WebSocket process, with GitHub Actions running Prisma generate, build and lint across both packages on every PR.

highlights.title: Server-authoritative by construction
highlights.detail: Clients can send only join_queue, make_move and leave_game. Every move is re-validated server-side for turn ownership, bounds and cell ownership and dropped silently when invalid, so a patched client cannot desync the room or forge a board.

highlights.title: A pure engine, enforced as a rule not a convention
highlights.detail: game.logic.ts is forbidden from importing ws, http, fs, state, handlers or the DB. That constraint keeps the cascade algorithm testable in isolation and makes every rules bug reproducible in a script that runs without a server or a database.

highlights.title: Cascades resolved as a bounded fixed point
highlights.detail: Explosions settle by repeatedly collecting every over-critical cell until none remain, guarded by a 2000-iteration safety break — so a rules bug degrades into a logged anomaly instead of an infinite loop that pins the event loop and takes every concurrent match down with it.

highlights.title: Persistence that cannot break the game
highlights.detail: Match history and XP are written after game_over has already reached the players; repository errors are logged and contained. The documented invariant is that Postgres going down loses statistics, not matches — and it is the reason writes were deliberately kept off the per-move path.

highlights.title: Pre-launch hardening pass
highlights.detail: Refuses to boot in production without a >=32-character JWT secret; WebSocket payload caps, ping/pong liveness, idle timeouts and global + per-IP connection caps; per-IP and global message-rate budgets; a reaper for abandoned rooms; helmet and a CORS allowlist; HS256-pinned JWTs with issuer/audience; and constant-work login that hashes a dummy password for unknown emails to close the user-enumeration timing channel.

highlights.title: Leaderboard integrity
highlights.detail: XP accrues only to authenticated players, scales with board size factor and opponent count, and is bounded by a velocity cap (10 matches per 10 minutes) plus a lobby -> active -> finished room state machine — so two accounts cannot spin instant matches to farm rank.

highlights.title: Reconnection that does not freeze the room
highlights.detail: A dropped authenticated player holds their seat for a 30-second grace window and resumes the same room on reconnect; when the window expires the server forfeits them cleanly and advances the turn, instead of stalling every other player on a move that will never arrive.

challenges.problem: During a cascade, a single cell can change hands several times within one move, so attributing captured orbs to "the player who clicked" silently produces wrong boards.
challenges.approach: Ownership propagates from the exploding cell's owner read at explosion time, re-evaluated on every iteration of the settle loop, and any cell drained to zero has its owner reset to null so a count-0 cell can never carry a stale owner.
challenges.outcome: Captured as a written invariant in the game-logic doc, with the reproducing case pinned in the standalone smoke script that runs on every change to the engine.

challenges.problem: Elimination means "owns zero cells", which is trivially true for every player on an empty board — a naive check ends the match on the opening move.
challenges.approach: The elimination sweep is gated behind turnCount >= players.length, giving every player a guaranteed first turn before anyone can be knocked out.
challenges.outcome: A one-line guard, but it is the kind of boundary condition that only surfaces at 2-player and 20-player extremes; it is documented as a rule rather than left as a magic comparison.

challenges.problem: Supabase's pooler cannot serve the runtime and the Prisma CLI from one connection string: migrations need session-mode features the transaction pooler does not expose, and node-postgres reads sslmode=require as full CA verification, which fails against Supabase's self-signed certificate.
challenges.approach: Split the concerns — runtime traffic on the transaction pooler (port 6543, sslmode=no-verify) and migrations on the session pooler (port 5432, sslmode=require) — with a plain-Postgres fallback so a clean checkout still runs fully offline.
challenges.outcome: Documented as the project's connection model, which turned a recurring class of "works locally, fails on migrate" incidents into a decision someone can read in one page.

personal.name: crisplogs (Python)
description: A PyPI package that replaces Python's verbose logging setup with a single setup_logging() call.

Features ANSI-colored output per log level, 4 box styles (default, short-fixed, short-dynamic, long-boxed), structured extras rendered as inline/json/pretty, dual console+file logging with automatic ANSI stripping, named loggers with inherited config, and a configurable LogFormatter for custom handlers.
Zero runtime dependencies, supports Python 3.8–3.13.

personal.name: crisplogs (Node.js)
description: An npm package that brings Python-style structured logging to Node.js backends with a single setupLogging() call.

Features ANSI-colored output per log level, 4 box styles (default, short-fixed, short-dynamic, long-boxed), structured extras rendered as inline/json/pretty, async file logging via WriteStream with automatic ANSI stripping, named loggers, pluggable custom handlers, and full TypeScript types.
Zero runtime dependencies, ships ESM + CJS builds.
